newsitem.title: CANADA: TCPL builds dams around Manitoba compressor.
newsitem.headline: TCPL builds dams around Manitoba compressor.

text.p: Rising flood waters along the Red River in southern Manitoba have TransCanada PipeLines Ltd working to protect a major compressor station outside Winnipeg, TransCanada Chief Executive George Watson said on Thursday.
But so far, the company had not cut natural gas deliveries to eastern Canada and the northern United States due to the severe flooding, Watson told reporters after TransCanada's annual meeting.

A big concern to the company is its Station 41 at Ile des Chenes, Manitoba, where gas is routed either east on its mainline or south to Emerson, Manitoba where it flows into the Great Lakes Gas Transmission system.
"We actually raised the dirt berm around it three or four feet and actually had a...second portable dam installed inside, so we've got two lines of defense there," he said.
A dirt berm is an earthen dam to block flood waters.
TransCanada is also closely monitoring soil movement in the region, which has the potential to cause a rupture.

Station 41 is southeast of Winnipeg and outside any protection that would be provided by the massive ditch that diverts much of the Red River water around Manitoba's capital city when river levels rise.
The natural gas market has feared the specter of pipeline and compressor shutdowns in the northern states and southern Manitoba since river levels began to reach dangerous levels this spring.
Despite rampant market rumors of problems amid the devestation, especially in North Dakota and Minnesota, pipeline companies have yet to report any flood-related outages.
Watson said that if TransCanada was forced to shut down Station 41, the gas could continue to flow on the pipelines, albeit without compressor horsepower added there.
